entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @sahandiranmehr

🔶According to data published by the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) and the Critical Threats Project (CTP), which is affiliated with AEI, a total of 1,530 locations across Iran were recorded in open sources as sites of airstrikes or attack-related explosions between February 28 and September 8, 2026 — 420 of them in Tehran. These figures represent a count of "reported locations," not the number of attacks or human casualties; that is, multiple reports may correspond to a single attack, and a single location may have been struck more than once. According to this map, 1,287 of the 1,530 recorded locations were reported during the first 40 days of the war, while only 13 were recorded between April 9 and June 7; then, in June and July, another wave of attacks emerged with 226 reported locations, 138 of which were in southern Iran, in areas below the 30th parallel. Meanwhile, areas such as Bushehr, Bandar Abbas, and Qeshm, which had been targeted before, once again stood out in the data from the second period. Of the total 1,530 cases, 544 are classified as confirmed airstrikes, 550 as reported attacks, and 436 as explosions captured on video; however, in 1,142 cases, the perpetrator of the attack is not identified in the published data. This dataset merely offers a picture of the geographic and temporal distribution of reported cases and, on its own, cannot show the extent of human and civilian damage from any given attack.@sahandiranmehr

entry.title: [sahandiranmehr] 🔶This film is one of the most valuable documents of Iran's contemporary…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @sahandiranmehr

🔶This film is one of the most valuable documents of Iran's contemporary history. It shows the speech of the first Iranian at the first meeting of the United Nations in January 1946 in London. The speaker is the representative of the Iranian government, Seyyed Hassan Taghizadeh. Many consider Taghizadeh to be Iran's first true intellectual. He was a multifaceted figure. He went on to serve as ambassador, parliamentarian, minister, and president of the Senate. Alongside politics, he was also a distinguished scholar and thinker. During his time in the political arena, Taghizadeh influenced many intellectuals. Many, moved by his ideas, turned toward Western civilization. However, ill-wishers branded him "Westoxicated" and leveled the worst accusations against him. But he loved his homeland and was beholden to no one. More than a prominent and influential politician, he was an influential intellectual. He was the first politician to boldly undertake "self-criticism" and critique his own behavior and words: "When the matter of Atabak's nomination for premiership became the talk of the town, I used everything at my disposal—from the sting of my tongue to the poison of my pen—to bring him down before his premiership. In my speeches, I turned him into an absolute evil who was coming to tear down the constitution. I portrayed all his services as treason. I made such a demon of him that the blood of listeners younger than myself would boil, and they would lose control and resort to violent acts. I need not have issued a decree for terrorism to be held responsible for it; to the same extent that I make the atmosphere heated and radical, I bear moral responsibility for the consequences. When we turn our political opponent into a monster, we must be aware of our intellectual and moral responsibility."... "All my life I am paying the price for when Mohammad Ali Shah came through the door of reconciliation with the constitutionalists, I dug in my heels and opposed it."... "In the first period of my life, when I rose up in strife and aggression, I made mistakes, and I had the courage to admit this mistake." ... "The constitutionalists did not even shy away from uttering insults against the honor and reputation of the Shah in the newspapers, and the Shah's response was to file a complaint with the court, but not only was the Shah's complaint not addressed, other constitutionalists attempted an unsuccessful assassination of the Shah. Sixty years on from those days, I cannot hide my regret over the failure to reach understanding with Mohammad Ali Shah" (Andisheh-ye Pouya, Issue 39). P.S.: The fifth of Mehr was Taghizadeh's birthday. From the Instagram of: Mehrdad Hojjati @sahandiranmehr

On the forty-sixth anniversary of the Ba'ath regime of Iraq's invasion of Iran, a specialized panel was held at the Khabar Online news agency to examine and analyze the dimensions, the underlying contexts, and the reasons behind the eight-year continuation of the war, centered on this question: "Why did the first Sacred Defense last 8 years?" The panel featured Mohammad Doroudian, researcher and narrator of Sacred Defense history; Jahangir Karami, professor of international relations; and Sahand Iranmehr, writer and researcher. The discussion explored the logic behind the war's continuation and its end across three main areas: "Iran's response to UN Security Council Resolution 479," "the period of the liberation of Khorramshahr and why the fighting continued," and "the turning point from the capture of Faw to the acceptance of Resolution 598" — which you can watch here. A member of the Israeli delegation is writing down the names of those who walked out of Netanyahu's speech! The United Nations was founded after the Second World War. Poor humanity, after all that bloodshed, came slightly to its senses and said to itself: Surely from now on we'll settle things through dialogue and diplomacy and sitting around a table — not with bombs and cannons and tanks. Now, however, Trump the American — who all this time was showing off the free world and democracy and human rights, and whose predecessors brought down the Iron Curtain with that same bluster — conjures hell before everyone's eyes from behind the podium, saying that if they don't listen to him he can annihilate an entire nation; Netanyahu hoists the pagers like a trophy of honor and tells his critics: "Coward" — and the most interesting scene of all is this: him imagining himself as the monitor and snitch of Khan Bala, ruler and cherry switch in hand, waiting to hand over to His Excellency the list of names of those who didn't sit at the master's whipping post and left the session, so he can light the pipe of the "bad ones."

Unless "always," "attack," and "my country" mean something else entirely, then Your Majesty, allow me to point out that your child has "always" been in favor of "attacking" "your country." Unless — God forbid — you're like Eshrat Khanom, our childhood neighbor, who whenever the neighbors complained about her child causing trouble, would say: "I'm just as fed up as you are." And when the neighbors said, "Then kindly pay for the damage from his fire-setting?" she'd say: "I'm fed up myself — why should I pay for that unruly brat?" And when the neighbors said, "Then at least since you're his mother, twist his ear," she'd say: "Now for the sake of a bottle, I should rip my child's liver out like the man-eating Hind?!" And finally, when they said, "How is it you say nothing to him and yet claim you're fed up too?" she'd say: "A person should turn into a dog before becoming a mother, rather than feed people this nonsense!"@sahandiranmehr
